379.t: Roberts and Latin material at private parties
379.s: Roberts played Latin items at society parties.
379.q: He played some of that in some of those parties. He used to fill in whatever you wanted around, you know what I mean? Fill in, he used to get a kick out of it. He used to get a kick out of me doing -- he'd improvise around.

379.s: Roberts led small parties for the rich and treated Bauza like a son.
379.q: Lucky Roberts, I played some of these private parties for the rich people. He used to play a whole lot of them, sometimes four piece, sometimes five pieces. You know what I mean. He was a very nice man, because -- oh, man, he was a short guy. He always used to be racing all the time.

28.t: Depression years and joining Lucky Roberts
28.s: As times got rough in 1931-32 Butler joined Lucky Roberts's society orchestra, which demanded classics, the latest numbers and impeccable deportment.
28.ch: Lucky Roberts, Armstrong and the big-band rivalries
28.q: very, very rough. So it got so rough until even Father Devine, he come into action. He's -- the apples was coming on the scene. It was rough, very, very rough. However, during that time I was very, very lucky. And after that, I think it was $100.00 and something then, but I wouldn't work because…

28.t: Playing society estates and yachts for Lucky Roberts
28.s: The nine-piece band played teas, dances and regattas on millionaires' estates, with members singing, plus anecdotes about a drunk trombonist and Lucky's 'demon' talk.
28.ch: Lucky Roberts, Armstrong and the big-band rivalries
28.q: (Inaudible) he would give a reception ---these were or something for this bunch of people /millionaires. Sometimes they would call them teas. He'd give it all out on the estate, everything, cricket and croquet and all that stuff. And we'd come in, you'd have tea and sherbert (inaudible). And then…

663.t: Christmas and New Year's parties; why he moved to New Orleans
663.s: Country parties at holidays and little pay, which is why he came to the city to earn money.
663.ch: Life in New Orleans and tunings

448.t: Bechet down and out before the school
448.s: The interviewer recalls Bechet's pressing shop in 1939 and his Nick's period; Wilber agrees.

286.t: Music at the Roof Garden, Chris Kelly, and leaving Piron
286.s: Roof Garden crowds wanted sweet Lombardo-style music not blues; Chris Kelly played jazz; Russ left Piron in 1930 for lower pay and the Depression.
286.q: Well, they played, they played, they played the modern music, now. He only had a band on the counter on the style of the lombardo. You see. And the people that go into the root garden was the type of people. It wasn't, you know, the people that wanted all these junk, you know. Blues and all that…

309.t: Playing private uptown parties and hauling a piano
309.s: He played parties for wealthy families, including one needing a piano that Sylvester hauled by truck.
309.q: We sure miss out of good times. Old man, Carl, that had his, uh, Royalty place out here. He lived at number 19, uh, or something out here, right off of the Main Street. Right off of Carrollton Avenue, in other words. And, uh... Audubon Street. Audubon Place. That's right here. No, not our town.…

1.t: Luckey Roberts and Ford Dabney playing for society millionaires
1.s: Roberts picked up two musicians in a chauffeured car to play for rich Long Island and Tuxedo Park families, as did Ford Dabney.
1.ch: Cab Calloway, Harlem and New York musicians
1.q: I used to hear Luckey Roberts. He'd be around the Rhythm Club. You'd see Luckey Roberts come up and pick up two musicians, and there would be a chauffeured car that would take him. He wore a tuxedo (?).

89.t: Black musicians downtown and society gigs with Lucky Roberts
89.s: Black bands worked downtown ballrooms and did private gigs for rich families, riding their private railroad cars.
89.ch: Fletcher, Wooding and the Harlem scene
89.q: Well, yes, sure we did. We worked the Roseland, I told you, we worked the Club Alabam, we worked what was formerly the Little Club. Negro musicians worked all over New York, all over New York, in the restaurants and the small clubs. They didn't work the Palais Royal -- that was the big one where…

70.t: Luckey Roberts, Ford Dabney and society pianists
70.s: Roberts and Dabney got the best society jobs for Black pianists, and Roberts wrote hit songs.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: Oh, well. Luckey Roberts, he was really the epitome of society pianists. He got the best jobs of any pianist in New York.

97.t: Lucky Roberts and society jobs for the rich
97.s: Scott plays dates with Roberts for wealthy patrons, on Cecil Smith's advice.
97.ch: Chick Webb, Lucky Roberts, Alex Jackson
97.q: So Lucky Roberts, he called me up and asked me, could I play some dates with him. Well, I'd heard of him. Lucky played for strictly rich people. Well, I had played for rich people on Fifth Avenue, because nothing but rich people used to live there. I played for rich people. But he had rich people…
